items.prompt: What does a test written first act like?
choices: A finish line fixed before the work starts
A receipt printed after the work is done
A decoration added once the code is finished
items.explanation: The test says what done means before any effort is spent, like a line painted on the track first.

items.prompt: Runner A stops when tired and says "done". What is missing?
choices: A faster pair of running shoes
A target defined before the run began
A longer track to run along every day
items.explanation: Without a target set in advance, wherever you stop counts as the finish, so you can never miss it.

items.prompt: In TDD, what do you write first for a new behavior?
choices: The full implementation
The documentation page
A test that fails
items.explanation: The failing test comes first. It is the finish line the code will then be written to reach.

items.prompt: Writing the assertion first forces you to decide what?
choices: What the function hands back
Which editor the team uses
How long the build will take
items.explanation: An assertion compares a result with an expectation, so the shape of the result must be known first.

items.prompt: A test written after the code mostly records what?
choices: What the user will need next
What the code already does
What the team agreed beforehand
items.explanation: Written afterwards, the expected value is usually copied from what the code returns, so it confirms rather than challenges.

items.prompt: Why is the assertion the first user of your function?
choices: It is the only caller the function will ever have
It decides who is allowed to use the function
It calls the function before anything else does
items.explanation: The test is the earliest code to call the function, so it feels any awkwardness in the interface first.

items.prompt: An assertion is awkward to write. What is that usually a sign of?
choices: The interface is probably awkward
The test tool is certainly broken
The feature is already finished
items.explanation: If the test has trouble using the function, other code will have trouble too. Better to notice it now.

items.prompt: Which is a test-first first step for a password checker?
choices: Write the logic that scores passwords
Assert what checking "short" should return
Add warning messages to the console output
items.explanation: Test-first starts by stating the expected result for a concrete input, before any logic exists.

items.prompt: Two engineers build the same password checker. One writes logic and then adds `console.warn` calls. The other writes `expect(check("short")).toEqual(...)` first. Both flag weak passwords correctly. Which claim is best supported?
choices: The first is wrong, because a program that prints a warning has not really detected anything
The second returns a value other code can reuse, since the assertion needed one
The second runs faster, because tests execute before the code itself does
They are identical, because both flag the same set of weak passwords
items.explanation: Both can be correct, but only the second had to decide on a returned value before writing logic. That value can feed a form, an API reply or another check, while printed text cannot.
items.reference:
Set the finish line before the run
test first: the target exists before the effort
code first: the target is wherever you stopped
the first assertion fixes what the function returns
Why: an assertion needs a result to compare, so writing it first forces the result's shape to be decided early.
items.learnMore:
Why the test comes first

A test written first defines "done" before any effort is spent. A test written afterwards mostly records what the code already does. The first assertion is also the first caller of your function, so awkward interfaces show up right away.

Common mistake

Treating tests written after the code as the same thing. They check the code, but they cannot pressure its design.
items.reflection: Think of a task outside coding where you were told what "done" looked like before you started. How did that change the way you worked?

items.prompt: A developer writes the whole function, then writes tests that all pass on the first run. Which TDD benefit is lost most clearly?
choices: The ability to rerun the tests after each later change to the code
The guarantee that every branch is covered by tests
The early moment where an awkward interface has to be faced
The chance to rename the function after release
items.explanation: The interface was already fixed when the tests were written, so any awkwardness had to be worked around rather than reshaped. Coverage is a separate matter and can be good or bad either way.

items.prompt: Which task is the closest match to painting the finish line first?
choices: Grading the worksheet after every student has finished
Printing extra copies of the worksheet in advance
Asking students which questions they found easy
Writing the answer key before drafting the worksheet
items.explanation: The answer key states what correct looks like before the questions are written, just as a test states the expected result before the code exists.

items.prompt: A developer runs the finished function, pastes its output into the expected value of a test, and sees green. What does that test most likely show?
choices: Only that the code still does what it did when pasted
That the function meets the requirement the user stated
That the interface is well designed for other callers
That every edge case was considered before pasting
items.explanation: The expected value came from the code, not from the requirement, so the test can only detect change. It cannot say whether the original behavior was right.

items.prompt: What is the order of the three TDD steps?
choices: Green, red, refactor
Red, green, refactor
Refactor, red, green
items.explanation: First a test fails (red), then it passes (green), then the code is tidied (refactor).

items.prompt: What does red mean in the loop?
choices: All of the tests pass already
The code is tidied up
A new test fails
items.explanation: Red means the new test fails, because the behavior it checks does not exist yet.

items.prompt: What does green mean in the loop?
choices: The test now passes
The test was deleted again
The code was tidied
items.explanation: Green means the current test passes, which is the signal to stop adding code for this step.

items.prompt: What happens in the refactor step?
choices: New behavior is added without a test
Code is tidied while tests keep passing
The failing test is removed
items.explanation: Refactor changes structure only. The passing tests are what tell you behavior did not move.

items.prompt: How much does one cycle cover?
choices: A whole feature
A whole release
One small behavior
items.explanation: Cycles stay small so a failing test points to a small recent change.

items.prompt: After a refactor, what comes next?
choices: The next behavior's failing test
A final release to users
Deleting all of the tests
items.explanation: The loop starts again with a new red test for the next small piece of behavior.

items.prompt: Which step cleans up duplication left by a quick fix?
choices: Red
Refactor
Green
items.explanation: Green is allowed to be a shortcut. Refactor is where duplication and awkward structure are removed.

items.prompt: Which step shows that a test is able to fail?
choices: Green
Refactor
Red
items.explanation: Seeing a test fail before the code exists proves it is capable of failing, which is what makes a later pass meaningful.

items.prompt: A new test fails with the message that the function is not defined. Which step is this, and is the failure useful?
choices: Green; it confirms the code compiles and the function was found
Red; it means the test is broken and must be deleted and rewritten
Red; it confirms the test can fail before any code exists
Refactor; it confirms behavior has not changed at all
items.explanation: Before any implementation the test should fail. That failure is the proof that the test is capable of failing, which is the point of the red step.
items.reference:
The three steps of the loop
RED: a new test fails (the test can fail)
GREEN: minimum code makes it pass
REFACTOR: tidy up, tests stay green
then the next small behavior
Why: each step guards against one specific failure: a test that cannot fail, untested code, and decaying structure.
items.learnMore:
Red, green, refactor

Red proves the test is able to fail. Green adds only what that test demands. Refactor improves structure while passing tests warn if behavior moves. One cycle covers one small behavior, then the loop starts again.

Common mistake

Skipping red because "I know it will fail", or skipping refactor because the tests are already green.
items.reflection: Think of a skill you learned by repeating a small cycle (try, check, polish). Which of your cycle's steps did you tend to skip, and what did skipping it cost?

items.prompt: A guard in the table reads "untested code, guesses about behavior nothing verified". Which step does it belong to?
choices: Red, by writing the failing test before running anything at all
Refactor, by renaming variables after the pass
Red, by writing several tests at the same time
Green, by writing only what the current test needs
items.explanation: Green is the step where extra code could sneak in. Limiting it to what the one failing test demands keeps every line tied to a test.

items.prompt: A developer makes a test pass, then immediately starts the next failing test, leaving a block of duplicated code behind. Which step was skipped, and what builds up?
choices: Refactor; duplication and awkward structure with no forcing function to fix them
Red; failing tests that were never actually run before moving on
Green; behavior that was never made to pass any test
Refactor; extra passing tests that slowly make the whole suite run longer
items.explanation: Without the refactor step, shortcuts taken in green stay in place. Nothing in the loop will go back for them later.

items.prompt: Why does the loop keep each cycle to a small behavior instead of a whole feature?
choices: A large feature cannot be expressed as an assertion at all in any test
When a test goes red, the cause lies in the few lines just changed
Small cycles guarantee that no bug can ever be introduced into the code
The test tool only allows one assertion per feature
items.explanation: Short steps keep feedback precise. A big step that goes red leaves a large area to search, which is the cost small cycles avoid.

then the next small behavior

items.prompt: In the green step, how much code do you write?
choices: Everything the feature will need
Whatever feels complete to you at the time
Just enough to pass the current test
items.explanation: Green is limited to what the one failing test demands, no more.

items.prompt: Why avoid extra code in the green step?
choices: No test shows it is needed or correct
The compiler refuses to accept the extra code
It makes the test run slower
items.explanation: Extra code is a guess about the future that nothing has checked.

items.prompt: A green step returns a placeholder for inputs no test covers. Acceptable?
choices: No, every input must be handled
Yes, nothing yet requires more
Only if the placeholder is commented out
items.explanation: Until a test asks about those inputs, the placeholder is exactly the minimum.

items.prompt: What is code written beyond the current test?
choices: A proven part of the design
A test written in disguise
A guess about a future need
items.explanation: No assertion backs it, so it is a guess whatever it looks like.

items.prompt: How should you add a new rule safely?
choices: Write a failing test for it first
Add the rule now and test it later
Add it to every function at once
items.explanation: The failing test proves the rule is needed and shows when it works.

items.prompt: A tiny change turns one test red. Where is the cause likely?
choices: Somewhere in the whole project
In the few lines just changed
In a test written last month
items.explanation: Small steps keep the search area small.

items.prompt: What is the goal of "minimum code to pass"?
choices: Make the final code as short as possible
Hide the unfinished features from users
Keep every line traceable to a test
items.explanation: It is about traceability, not about brevity. Later refactoring can reshape the code.

items.prompt: After cycle 1, the function returns score 0 and no feedback for any non-empty password. Why is that fine?
choices: No test yet asks about non-empty input
The checker never receives real passwords
Placeholders are always required by the loop here
items.explanation: The function only has to meet the tests that exist so far. The next test will force the next piece.

items.prompt: The only failing test says an empty password returns the "required" message. While there, the developer also writes the length and uppercase checks. What is true afterwards?
choices: Those two checks are verified by the empty-password test that ran
Those two checks can now never contain a mistake
The empty-password test no longer needs to be run
Those two checks exist although no test demands or verifies them
items.explanation: The test checks only the empty case. The extra checks are unverified guesses and nothing would turn red if they were wrong.
items.reference:
What green is allowed to write
current failing test: the only demand
code beyond it: a bet on a future need
no test behind a line: nothing can verify it
need more behavior? write its red test first
Why: keeping each line traceable to a test means nothing in the code is unverified guesswork.
items.learnMore:
Minimum code to pass

In green, write just enough for the current test. A placeholder for inputs no test covers is fine, since nothing yet requires it to be correct. When behavior is needed, a failing test for it comes first. Minimum does not mean sloppy, because refactor is the step that tidies.

Common mistake

Adding "just in case" branches. They look harmless, but with no test they can be wrong for months without anyone noticing.
items.reflection: Where in your own work do you build "just in case" extras before anyone asked? What would it look like to wait until a concrete need appeared?

items.prompt: After cycle 1, a placeholder returns score 0 for every non-empty password. The next test expects "short" to get the length message. What should happen?
choices: The new test goes red, then the placeholder is replaced by the least code that satisfies it
The new test is edited so that the old placeholder still passes it
The full set of future rules is written all at once, before the next run
The placeholder is kept and the message is hard-coded in another file
items.explanation: A placeholder is meant to be outgrown. The red test is what forces the next small piece of real logic.

items.prompt: Why is "minimum code to pass" not the same as "write sloppy code"?
choices: Sloppy code is permitted because the tests will find all the errors later
Refactor is the step that cleans structure, so green can stay small
Green code is exempt from review once its test passes
The loop forbids any clean-up until the whole feature is done
items.explanation: Minimum describes what behavior green adds. Structure is handled in the next step while the passing tests guard behavior.

items.prompt: A "just in case" check for missing input is added though no test sends missing input. Months later it contains a bug. Why did nothing catch it?
choices: Tests are unable to cover code that handles missing input
The bug only appears after enough months have passed
No test ever exercised it, so nothing could turn red
Branches that never run are removed automatically
items.explanation: Code with no assertion behind it has no way to fail a test. The bug can sit there until real input arrives.

items.prompt: A function that returns a value is easy to do what with?
choices: Compare in an assertion
Hide from every test
Run only once per day
items.explanation: An assertion can compare the returned value with the expected one directly.

items.prompt: A function that only prints is hard to do what with?
choices: Call from the console
Assert against directly
Read as text by a person
items.explanation: The result lives in text on a screen, not in a value an assertion can compare.

items.prompt: What does design pressure mean here?
choices: Managers pushing the team to ship faster each week
Deadlines forcing the team to write fewer tests
Writing the assertion first nudges the interface toward testable shapes
items.explanation: The pressure comes from the order of work, not from anyone.

items.prompt: When is an awkward interface noticed under TDD?
choices: When the assertion is written
Only after the release ships
Never, the awkwardness stays hidden
items.explanation: Writing the assertion means using the interface first, which exposes the awkwardness at once.

items.prompt: An easy-to-test design is usually what else?
choices: Impossible to change at all later
Easy to reuse elsewhere
Limited to one screen
items.explanation: A function with inputs in and a value out is easy to test and easy to call from anywhere.

items.prompt: Which return is easier to reuse across a form and an API?
choices: A line of text printed to the console log
A sound played whenever a rule fails
A result object with score and feedback
items.explanation: A structured result can be shown, sent or checked by any caller.

items.prompt: What did the first assertion in the checker decide?
choices: The result is an object with score and feedback
The checker is written in one certain editor
The checker will print its output to a screen
items.explanation: To compare anything, the test needed a result with a defined shape.

items.prompt: Can code-first work reach a testable design?
choices: No, never under any circumstance
Yes, but nothing pressures it early
Only if tests are never written
items.explanation: It can, but without an assertion waiting, an untestable shape feels fine until later.

items.prompt: Four checkers are proposed. Which is hardest to assert against?
choices: One that writes its complaints to a shared log file
One that returns an ordered list of complaint messages
One that returns an object with ok and errors
One that returns true or false for the password
items.explanation: The result goes to a side channel, so the test must read the log and filter out other entries. The others return values the assertion can compare directly.
items.reference:
What an assertion can grab onto
returns a value: assertion compares it directly
only prints: assertion must capture and parse text
easiest to test and easiest to reuse: the same design
code first can get there, but nothing pushes early
Why: an interface that is hard to assert against is felt at the moment the assertion is written, before other code depends on it.
items.learnMore:
Testability as design pressure

Because the assertion is written first, the function has to return something it can compare. A function that returns structured data can also feed a form, an API reply or another check. Writing code first can land on the same design, but nothing forces the question early.

Common mistake

Believing TDD guarantees good design. It brings the awkward interface into view early, and you still have to act on it.
items.reflection: Think of a tool or a form you use that was clearly built without anyone trying it first. What awkwardness would a first attempt to use it have exposed?

items.prompt: A teammate says TDD makes designs good automatically. What is the best response?
choices: That is right, because passing tests prove the design is a good one
It forces an awkward interface into view early, but fixing it is still your choice
That is wrong, because the tests have no connection to design
That is right, as long as the tests are run on every commit
items.explanation: The loop provides the early moment of friction. A weak design with loosely written tests can still pass forever.

items.prompt: Suppose the first test had been `expect(isValidPassword("")).toBe(false)`. How would that have shaped the design?
choices: The function would be forced to return a score and a list of messages at once
The function would be forced to print the reasons instead
A boolean cannot say which rule failed, so feedback needs a later redesign
Nothing would differ, because booleans carry all information
items.explanation: The first assertion fixes the result's shape. A boolean can only say yes or no, and the need for messages would force a change to every caller later.

items.prompt: To check a function, a test has to capture what it printed to the console and search the text. What does that suggest?
choices: The function is well designed for reuse in other places, such as an API
The test tool is missing a required feature
The function must be rewritten in another language
Its result is tangled with display, a sign the interface is awkward
items.explanation: Needing to capture and parse display text means there is no clean value to assert on. That friction is exactly the signal TDD is meant to surface.

items.prompt: During a refactor, what should happen to behavior?
choices: It gains new features
It stays the same
It is rewritten from scratch
items.explanation: Refactoring is a change of structure only, with identical behavior.

items.prompt: What guards a refactor from changing behavior?
choices: Good intentions and a careful read
A longer code review before merging
Passing tests
items.explanation: If a change alters checked behavior, a test goes red right away.

items.prompt: A test fails right after a refactor. What does that suggest?
choices: Behavior probably changed
The refactor was a clear success
The test can be deleted
items.explanation: A refactor should not turn tests red. A failure points to a behavior change you did not intend.

items.prompt: Should a refactor add new features?
choices: Yes, if they are small
No, features need their own failing test
Yes, whenever the code is open
items.explanation: New behavior belongs in a red-green cycle, not hidden inside a refactor.

items.prompt: A refactor is only as safe as what?
choices: The length of the code in lines
The age of the project overall
The behavior the tests pin down
items.explanation: Tests can only warn about behavior they actually assert.

items.prompt: Why not skip refactor once the test passes?
choices: Shortcuts from green pile up as duplication
The loop ends right before refactor
Passing tests clean the code on their own
items.explanation: Green may leave messy code behind. Refactor is where it gets cleaned.

items.prompt: Three if/else checks become one rule list. What must stay the same?
choices: The number of lines in the code
The results for the same inputs
The names of the variables

No, tests prove nothing
Only for the behavior they check
items.explanation: A test can only notice a change in what it looks at.

choices: Nothing in the function's behavior has changed
Nothing those three tests check has changed
The new structure is certainly better than the old one was
The function is now fully covered by tests
items.explanation: A clean run only covers what the tests assert. Behavior outside them could have moved without a single red.

refactor changes structure, not behavior

What refactoring is safe against

Because passing tests turn red when checked behavior changes, you can restructure boldly. The safety has a limit: it covers the behavior the tests assert, not the behavior they happen to ignore. A looser assertion, such as a length check on a list, lets order mistakes through.

items.prompt: Does the loop change for a new requirement?
choices: Yes, tests are skipped for it
Yes, refactor comes first
No, it is red, green, refactor again
items.explanation: The loop is the same for any behavior, big or small.

items.prompt: What is the first step to reject common passwords?
choices: Write a failing test for it
Add a list of common passwords to the code
Delete the old tests
items.explanation: The failing test states the new behavior before any code is written.

items.prompt: With the rule list only, what score does "password123" get?
items.explanation: It passes the length and number rules and fails only the uppercase rule, so the score is 2.

items.prompt: Why check for common passwords before the rules?
choices: Rules cannot run on very short text
It makes the code a bit harder to read
A common password should not earn partial credit
items.explanation: Running the rules first would give "password123" a score of 2 for being long enough, which defeats the point.

items.prompt: Does the test decide which design to use?
choices: No, it only checks the design you pick
Yes, it always picks the best one
Yes, it always picks the simplest
items.explanation: Several designs can pass the same test. Choosing between them remains your call.

items.prompt: A rule does not fit the check-and-message shape. What first?
choices: Skip the test until the very end
Write its test, then choose a design that passes
Force it into the old check-message shape
items.explanation: The test is written first regardless, and the design follows from what it has to satisfy.

items.prompt: How do you know the new test is red for a real reason?
choices: The test file has no syntax errors in it
The editor shows the test name in red
The old function returns score 2, not 0
items.explanation: The failure comes from a different result, not from a mistake in the test.

items.prompt: What stays the same when the requirement changes shape?
choices: A concrete test validates the chosen design
The design always stays unchanged
The tests become optional
items.explanation: Whatever design you pick, a specific test exists to prove it.

items.prompt: With the rule list as it stands, what does "password123" return, and what must the first step for the new "too common" requirement achieve?
choices: Score 0 with three messages; a green test that already passes today
Score 3 with no messages; a refactor that merges the rules into one
Score 2 with one message; a red test expecting score 0 and the "too common" message
Score 2 with one message; a new rule appended to the list
items.explanation: The list gives 2 for length and number and one message for uppercase. The new test expects 0 and a different message, so it must start red.
items.reference:
A requirement that breaks the shape
new rule: failing test first, as always
"password123" with the rule list: score 2, not 0
early return before the rules gives score 0
the test checks the choice, it does not make it
Why: the loop guarantees a concrete test for whichever design you choose, but it does not choose the design.
items.learnMore:
When the next requirement is different

A requirement that does not fit the check-and-message shape does not change the loop. The red test shows the current design fails for a real reason, and the least code that passes may mean a short-circuit before the rule list. Several designs may pass, and choosing between them is judgment.

Common mistake

Thinking a passing test proves the chosen design is the best one. It only proves that the design does what the test says.
items.reflection: Think of a rule at work or in a game that did not fit the existing system. Who decided how to handle it, and what test (formal or not) told you the choice worked?

items.prompt: Make this assertion pass: `describeEmpty("")` returns `{ score: 0, feedback: ["Password is required"] }`, and any non-empty text returns `{ score: 0, feedback: [] }`.
items.explanation: The empty case returns the required message, and the placeholder covers everything else, which is exactly the minimum cycle 1 asks for.

items.prompt: Write `longEnough(p)`: true when the password has 8 or more characters, false otherwise.
items.explanation: The boundary is 8 inclusive, so 8 characters pass and 7 do not.

items.prompt: Write `hasUppercase(p)`: true when the password contains at least one capital letter A to Z.
items.explanation: A character class from A to Z tests for any capital letter.

items.prompt: Write `hasNumber(p)`: true when the password contains at least one digit.
items.explanation: A character class from 0 to 9 tests for any digit.

items.prompt: Write `lengthFeedback(p)`: `[]` when the password has 8 or more characters, otherwise `["Add more characters (min 8)"]`.
items.explanation: A passing rule contributes no message and a failing one contributes its message in a list.

items.prompt: Write `scoreOf(results)`: given an array of true/false rule results, return how many are true.
items.explanation: The score counts passed rules, so it is the number of true values.

items.prompt: Write `failedMessages(results, messages)`: return the messages whose matching result is false, keeping their order.
items.explanation: Messages are paired with results by position, and filtering keeps the original order.

items.prompt: Write `isTooCommon(p, list)`: true when the password appears exactly in the list of common passwords.
items.explanation: An exact membership check against the list is all the rule needs.

items.prompt: Implement `describePasswordStrength(password)`. Empty gives `{ score: 0, feedback: ["Password is required"] }`. Otherwise run three rules in this order: 8 or more characters ("Add more characters (min 8)"), an uppercase letter ("Add an uppercase letter"), a digit ("Add a number"). Score is the number of rules passed; feedback lists messages of rules failed, in rule order.

tests.expr: expect(describePasswordStrength("short")).toEqual({ score: 0, feedback: ["Add more characters (min 8)", "Add an uppercase letter", "Add a number"] })
expect(describePasswordStrength("longenough")).toEqual({ score: 1, feedback: ["Add an uppercase letter", "Add a number"] })

items.explanation: Empty input returns early. Each rule either adds one to the score or contributes its message, in the order the rules are listed, which is what the exact array comparison checks.
items.reference:
From assertions to a rule loop
empty input: early return with the required message
each rule: check passes = score + 1, else its message
feedback keeps the order the rules run in
same inputs, same outputs, before and after refactor
Why: every branch exists because an assertion demanded it, so the function can be rebuilt from its tests.
items.learnMore:
Writing the checker from its tests

Read the assertions as the spec. Each failed rule contributes its message in rule order, each passed rule adds one to the score, and empty input short-circuits. Here, writing the code is the understanding, because the order and exactness of the output is what the tests pin down.

Common mistake

Returning messages in a different order, or counting score from failures instead of passes. Both look reasonable but fail the exact comparison.
items.reflection: Think of a procedure you could write as a short list of rules (a recipe, a packing list). Which rule would you add next, and what would the test for it say?

items.prompt: Implement `describePasswordStrength(password)` with these rules, in order: 10 or more characters ("Use at least 10 characters"), a lowercase letter ("Add a lowercase letter"), a digit ("Add a number"). Empty input gives `{ score: 0, feedback: ["Password is required"] }`. Score counts rules passed; feedback lists failed messages in rule order.

tests.expr: expect(describePasswordStrength("ABC")).toEqual({ score: 0, feedback: ["Use at least 10 characters", "Add a lowercase letter", "Add a number"] })

items.explanation: The structure is the same with different rules. The nine-character case sits just under the new boundary, which is why it fails only the length rule.

items.prompt: Implement `describePasswordStrength(password, common)`. If the password is in the `common` array, return `{ score: 0, feedback: ["This password is too common"] }` before anything else. tests.expr: expect(describePasswordStrength("password123", ["password123"])).toEqual({ score: 0, feedback: ["This password is too common"] })

items.explanation: The common check runs first and returns early, so a common password earns no partial credit from the rules. The remaining behavior is the ordinary rule loop unrolled.

items.prompt: Implement `runRules(password, rules)`, the refactored core. `rules` is an array of `{ check, message }` where `check` is a function. Return `{ score, feedback }`: score is how many checks returned true, feedback lists messages of failed checks in the order of `rules`. With an empty `rules` array, return `{ score: 0, feedback: [] }`.

tests.expr: expect(runRules("ab", [{ check: (p) => p.length > 1, message: "m1" }, { check: (p) => p === "z", message: "m2" }])).toEqual({ score: 1, feedback: ["m2"] })
expect(runRules("a", [{ check: () => false, message: "first" }, { check: () => false, message: "second" }])).toEqual({ score: 0, feedback: ["first", "second"] })
expect(runRules("a", [{ check: () => true, message: "x" }])).toEqual({ score: 1, feedback: [] })

items.explanation: A single loop replaces the repeated if/else blocks. Because it is generic over the rule list, new rules are data rather than new code paths.
